If your Social Security check currently lands at $1,500 a month, you've probably already heard that a raise is coming in 2027. The Social Security Administration (SSA) has confirmed the exact percentage, and the number is bigger than last year's increase.  But turning a percentage into real dollars in your bank account is where things get confusing for a lot of retirees who rely on Social Security to cover retirement expenses and eliminate some money stress . The gap between what SSA announces and what actually shows up as a deposit trips people up every year. Medicare premiums, tax withholding, and SSA's rounding rules can all nudge the final number away from a simple back-of-the-envelope calculation. Here's how to work through the math for a $1,500 benefit, when the new amount actually starts, and what might explain why your bank deposit doesn't match it exactly. Read More Here › SPONSORED The confirmed 2027 COLA and what it means in dollars The SSA announced on October 14, 2026, that Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits would rise by 3.6% in 2027 , according to the agency's official press release.  This cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation, and it's calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For 2027, the COLA reflects the CPI-W increase from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026, per SSA's official COLA computation page. For a $1,500 monthly benefit, a 3.6% increase works out to an additional $54 a month, bringing the gross benefit to approximately $1,554. Over a full year, that's about $648 in additional gross income.  This is a simplified example based on the raw 3.6% figure. Your actual increase could land a few dollars above or below this estimate once SSA applies its official rounding rules, which round any COLA percentage to the nearest tenth of one percent and round final dollar benefit amounts accordingly. For context, SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet shows that the average retired worker's benefit would rise from $2,095 to $2,170 a month, an increase of about $75, which lines up with the agency's overall projection that retirement benefits would climb by roughly that amount on average starting in January. Your own increase depends on your personal benefit amount, not the average. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. When the higher payment actually begins The 3.6% COLA takes effect with benefits payable in January 2027, according to SSA. Retirement, survivor, and Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) beneficiaries would see the new amount in their January payment, which follows the standard birth-date payment schedule.  SSI recipients are on a different calendar: because SSI's normal payment date is the first of the month and January 1, 2027, is a holiday, the increased SSI payment arrives on December 31, 2026, SSA's COLA information page confirms. This timing trips people up because SSI recipients would technically see their raise before the calendar flips to the new year, while retirement beneficiaries wait until their regular January payment date. A practical budgeting example Say your current gross Social Security benefit is $1,500 a month. After the 3.6% COLA, your gross benefit is approximately $1,554. If you don't have Medicare premiums or tax withholding deducted from your check, that extra $54 could go straight into your bank account. But many retirees have deductions that change the picture. For example, someone enrolled in Medicare Part B has that premium deducted directly from their Social Security payment. The 2027 Part B standard premium had not been announced by CMS as of this writing, so it's worth checking a COLA notice or the Medicare.gov website once the new amount is published rather than assuming last year's premium would carry over unchanged.  If the Part B premium rises at the same time a gross benefit rises, a net deposit increase could be smaller than $54,  or in some cases, barely noticeable. Retirees who have federal income tax voluntarily withheld from their benefit, or who pay a Medicare Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) because of higher income, would see their own unique combination of increases and deductions. IRMAA is based on income reported on a tax return from two years prior, per SSA guidance.  There's no single outcome that applies to everyone: someone with no Medicare deduction and no tax withholding might see nearly the full $54 bump, while someone with multiple deductions might see a more modest change. A useful approach is comparing last year's net deposit to a new COLA notice line-by-line, rather than assuming the raise applies evenly across every household. Learn More Here › SPONSORED Why a bank deposit might not match the gross COLA math The $54 figure in this example reflects the increase to the gross benefit, which is the amount before any deductions. The net payment, which is what actually lands in a bank account, depends on what's subtracted. Common deductions include: Medicare Part B premiums (and Part D premiums, if withheld).  IRMAA surcharges for higher-income beneficiaries, based on income reported on a tax return from two years prior.  Voluntary federal tax withholding.  Garnishments for certain debts, such as unpaid federal taxes or court-ordered support. Because Medicare premium changes typically take effect in January as well, many retirees see their Part B premium and their COLA increase applied in the same month, which could make the net change feel smaller than the gross percentage suggests. This isn't a reduction in the raise so much as two separate adjustments landing at once. How to find a personalized COLA notice Rather than relying on an estimate, SSA provides each beneficiary with a simplified, one-page COLA notice that spells out the exact new gross benefit, any deductions, and the net payment amount, according to the SSA press release announcing the 2027 COLA increase.  People with a personal My Social Security account could view this notice online starting in late November 2026, which SSA says is up to three weeks earlier than a mailed notice arrives. To see the notice online, SSA says individuals generally need to have created an account and opted into paperless notices by November 18, 2026. Anyone who hasn't opted into paperless notices would receive a mailed notice in December 2026. Checking a personalized notice is the most reliable way to know specific 2027 numbers, since it reflects individual benefit history, any Medicare premiums paid, and any withholding set up, rather than a generic average. Bottom line A 3.6% COLA sounds straightforward, but the gap between a gross benefit increase and an actual deposit depends on details unique to each situation, including Medicare premiums and any tax withholding. A $1,500 benefit becoming roughly $1,554 is a reasonable starting estimate, but it's the gross figure, not necessarily what lands in a bank account. For exact numbers, a personalized COLA notice, available through a my Social Security account or in the mail, is the authoritative source. Anyone with questions about specific deductions or payment amounts once the notice arrives could contact SSA's customer service line or a local field office for clarification. Once you know the net amount, you could decide whether you need to boost a fixed income . FAQs Can a higher Medicare Part B premium cancel out my COLA? For most people, no. A "hold harmless" rule says that for people whose Part B premium is deducted from their Social Security check, the dollar increase in the premium can't exceed the dollar increase in their COLA, so their net benefit doesn't fall. It doesn't protect people who are new to Medicare, who pay an income-related surcharge (IRMAA), or whose premium is billed directly rather than deducted.  Could I qualify for help with Medicare premiums if my benefit is around $1,500? Possibly. For 2026, the Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) program has a monthly income limit of $1,616 for an individual (including a $20 disregard) and a resource limit of $9,950. If Social Security is your only income, a $1,500 benefit, or about $1,554 after the COLA, falls below that limit, and SLMB pays your Part B premium. Limits update each year with the federal poverty guidelines, and states can set more generous rules, so check with your state Medicaid office. Could the COLA affect my SNAP, Medicaid, or housing assistance? It can. Social Security counts as income for SNAP, so a COLA can lower your monthly food benefit or, if it pushes your income over the limit, end it, though the reduction is typically much smaller than the raise. Medicaid timing varies by state: Pennsylvania advocates note that the COLA generally shouldn't count against Medicaid eligibility for the first few months of the year, until the new poverty levels are published. Rent in income-based housing can also rise. Tell each program about your new benefit amount promptly, and appeal if a decision looks wrong.
